questions.q: What is a branch protection rule?
options: A setting that encrypts a branch's contents
A restriction, set by a repository administrator, on what can happen to a specific branch regardless of who's trying
A type of merge conflict
A required naming convention for branches
questions.explain: Branch protection rules restrict behaviors like direct pushes, force-pushes, or merging without review/passing checks on a specific branch (usually main), regardless of who is attempting it.

questions.q: What problem does "require branches to be up to date before merging" specifically prevent?
options: A reviewer approving a PR without reading it
A PR merging against a now-stale version of main, introducing a regression the reviewer never actually saw
Two branches having the same name
A commit message being too long
questions.explain: If main has moved on since a PR was reviewed, merging without first updating the PR's branch can introduce changes that interact badly with what's now on main — changes the reviewer approved a different version of main against.

questions.q: Which repository role allows pushing branches and opening/merging PRs, but not changing branch protection rules?
options: Read
Triage
Write
Admin
questions.explain: Write access lets a collaborator push branches and open/merge PRs that pass protection rules, but changing the protection rules themselves requires Admin (or in some cases Maintain for non-sensitive settings).

questions.q: If a repository requires at least one reviewer's approval before merging, can a collaborator with Write access merge their own unreviewed PR?
options: Yes, Write access always overrides branch protection rules
No — branch protection can block merging even for someone with Write access, until the approval requirement is met
Only if they are the repository's original creator
Only on weekends
questions.explain: Repository role and branch protection work together: Write access lets you propose a change, but a protection rule requiring approval can still block you from merging it yourself until that requirement is satisfied.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say branch protection matters even more once a Git repo is the source of truth for Salesforce metadata?
options: Because Salesforce requires branch protection to be enabled by law
Because an unreviewed push to main could push an unvalidated metadata change toward a real production org, bypassing review or validation steps
Because Salesforce orgs cannot connect to unprotected repositories at all
Because branch protection automatically deploys metadata to production
questions.explain: Once the repo drives what gets deployed to a real org, an unreviewed/unchecked push to main isn't just messy history — it's an unvetted change heading toward production, which is exactly what branch protection is meant to prevent.
